title: Divine Presence
summary: These passages picture God’s presence in several ways. In Exodus 3, God addresses Moses from the burning bush and identifies as the God of his ancestors. At the end of Exodus, a cloud covers the tent of meeting and God’s glory fills it; in 1 Kings 8 the cloud fills Solomon’s temple at its dedication. John 1 says the Word became flesh and lived among people, while Revelation 21 pictures God dwelling with humanity in a renewed creation. The theme links call, sanctuary, temple, incarnation, and future hope, but the texts do not describe one identical kind of presence in every setting.
historical_context: The references move through different narrative and visionary settings. In Exodus 3, Moses encounters the divine presence at the bush on Horeb; in Exodus 40, the completed tent is covered by cloud and filled with glory. First Kings 8 narrates the dedication of Solomon’s temple and the cloud that fills the house. John 1 places the Word’s dwelling among people in the opening of a Gospel, and Revelation 21 presents God’s dwelling with humanity in a vision of renewed creation. These scenes connect presence with different places and purposes rather than recording a single continuous historical event.
canonical_context: Exodus 3 portrays God addressing Moses at the bush; Exodus 40 and 1 Kings 8 describe the cloud and glory filling the tent and temple. John 1 speaks of the Word living among people, and Revelation 21 envisions God dwelling with humanity. The sequence connects divine presence with calling, Israel’s worship spaces, the Gospel’s account of Jesus, and hope for renewed creation. Each passage uses the theme differently, so the later texts should not erase the earlier settings.
literary_context: The theme appears in narrative scenes in Exodus and Kings, a theological opening in John, and an apocalyptic vision in Revelation. In Exodus 3 Moses turns aside to the bush and hides his face; Exodus 40 closes the tabernacle instructions with cloud and glory; 1 Kings 8 recounts the temple dedication. John 1 opens with the Word’s presence among people, while Revelation 21 brings the theme into a vision of God dwelling with humanity. These literary forms present presence as encounter, worship, incarnation, and hope.
covenantal_significance: The passages portray presence as a relationship and promise, not only as a location. God meets Moses at the bush; the cloud and glory accompany Israel’s tent and later fill Solomon’s temple; John 1 presents the Word living among people; Revelation 21 promises God’s dwelling with humanity. Together, the texts connect divine presence with calling, communal worship, and future hope. They do not require readers to treat a bush, tent, temple, incarnation, and final vision as the same kind of event.
canonical_role: Divine Presence serves as a theological anchor, connecting doctrinal concepts, canonical development, and related passages across Scripture.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Divine Presence in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
